articles.body:
El presidente no hace distinción entre Feijóo y su socio potencial de Gobierno y destaca las alianzas del líder de Vox con dirigentes de la ultraderecha global como Trump, Milei, Orban, Salvini y Meloni

Pedro Sánchez ha pedido este sábado, en el mitin del PSOE en Palma de Mallorca, “el voto de todos los europeístas que quieren más Europa y no menos Europa”, en contraposición al respaldo que Santiago Abascal ha obtenido de algunos de los dirigentes ultras del continente que más destacan por su antieuropeísmo, como el húngaro Viktor Orbán y el italiano Matteo Salvini. El 70% de los españoles son afines a la Unión Europea, según el Eurobarómetro de 2024, en el que se preguntaba de forma expresa por ese vínculo, superando la media europea del 63%.

El presidente ha apelado en el acto, que ha congregado a más de 5.000 personas según la organización, a los ciudadanos que, con independencia de su ideología, “quieren una solución a las crisis” como la que el Gobierno dio en 2020 en la pandemia “con fondos europeos y no con el austericidio al que sometió la derecha y la ultraderecha durante la crisis financiera a los países del sur de Europa, entre ellos España”. Sánchez logró que España fuese el país que recibiese más fondos de Bruselas para combatir el impacto de la covid en la peor crisis sanitaria en un siglo, tan solo por detrás de Italia.

La relación del candidato de Vox con los referentes de la ultraderecha mundial ha sido uno de los hilos conductores del mitin, en el que no se han hecho distinciones entre Abascal y Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “Lo que no queremos para el mundo, no lo queramos para nuestro país”, ha recalcado Sánchez, que ha recordado el triunfo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva en Brasil frente a los socios de Abascal y, por tanto, de Feijóo, según La Moncloa y Ferraz. “¿Qué representan Feijóo y Abascal? No representan una alternativa de nada porque no ofrecen nada salvo los recortes y la motosierra", ha aseverado el candidato del PSOE. Había previsto un diálogo el lunes entre Sánchez y Lula en la sede de UGT en Madrid, en otro guiño hacia los sindicatos tras los ataques que les ha dedicado la derecha por la huelga general, pero se ha suspendido porque el presidente latinoamericano sufre una afonía.

📺 TV EN DIRECTO | Sánchez: "¿Es que Trump ha significado para la sociedad estadounidense una alternativa o una involución? [...] Lo que no queremos para el mundo no lo queramos para nuestro país" https://t.co/d93IApZBP2 pic.twitter.com/4htbMy34PI

— EL PAÍS (@el_pais) November 14, 2026

A juicio de Sánchez, los líderes de PP y Vox “representan los mismos insultos, las mismas mentiras y los mismos recortes que la familia a la que pertenecen: la internacional ultraderechista liderada por Trump, por Milei y por Bolsonaro, por Le Pen, Meloni, Salvini y Orbán”, ha sentenciado. La primera ministra italiana ha mostrado su apoyo a Abascal en un vídeo difundido en un acto de Vox en la Plaza de Colón de Madrid: “Conoces la estima y el afecto que te tengo. Estoy segura de que seguirás defendiendo tus ideas con pasión y la determinación de siempre (...) Me gustaría mucho poder colaborar contigo a otro nivel”, le dedica. Sánchez ha aprovechado ese soporte para alertar del “apoyo más granado de la extrema derecha antieuropeísta” a Abascal.

Decreto ‘Maricarmen’ frente al ‘aticazo’ de Ayuso

El secretario general del PSOE ha centrado su tercer mitin de campaña en una de las 18 circunscripciones prioritarias en las que los socialistas se juegan las elecciones, en denunciar “la mala educación” del PP y Vox y responsabilizarles de ser los causantes del ambiente polarizado en el Congreso de los Diputados. El presidente ha destacado cómo en los tres años que Francina Armengol ha sido la presidenta del Parlamento “ha visto cómo el insulto tapaba sus ansias en el Congreso, cómo la falta de argumentos, cómo el ruido, cómo el grito se trataban de imponer a aquellos que planteábamos soluciones a los problemas reales de los ciudadanos y ciudadanas”. Sánchez le ha agradecido a Armengol que, como presidenta, “haya mantenido la calma y defendido la buena educación en el debate público” en la Cámara baja.

📺 TV EN DIRECTO | Sánchez dedica unas palabras a Armengol: "Has defendido la buena educación en el debate público del Congreso de los Diputados, frente a tanto ataque injustificado de la derecha" https://t.co/d93IApZ3Zu pic.twitter.com/QfTyVji4aH

— EL PAÍS (@el_pais) November 14, 2026

La presidenta del Congreso y secretaria general de los socialistas de Baleares se ha declarado “muy orgullosa” de que en su etapa como tercera autoridad del Estado se haya aprobado en el Parlamento el uso de las lenguas cooficiales “y se hablase en catalán, euskera y gallego” de forma cotidiana en las sesiones parlamentarias. “Y va el PP, Feijóo, y dice que será lo primero que quitará”, ha advertido en su intervención, en la que ha combinado el castellano y el catalán. La expresidenta autonómica (2015-2023) ha recalcado que Sánchez “es la persona más fuerte” que conoce y que el 29-N “se vota también contra la mala educación de PP y Vox”, como ha señalado Sánchez. “No es que el país esté polarizado, es que algunos no aceptaron el resultado electoral, y van a rabiar porque Sánchez va a volver a ser el presidente”, ha apostillado. “No hay una polarización, hay un clima de agresividad buscado”, afirmó el mes pasado en una entrevista en EL PAÍS.

En una comunidad donde la crisis de la vivienda es uno de los grandes dramas sociales, Sánchez ha interpelado al PP y a Vox por su rechazo a la aprobación del decreto de vivienda denominado simbólicamente como decreto Maricarmen por la anciana desahuciada en septiembre en Madrid y que falleció en el hospital sin poder regresar al piso de renta antigua en el que vivió siete décadas. “¿Qué objeción tienen?”, ha incidido, enfundado en una camiseta con el mensaje en catalán La força de la gent. El presidente ha reprochado que Feijóo “avale” la compra del “aticazo” para la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, en referencia a la polémica compra por 6,3 millones de euros en la que el Tribunal de Cuentas ha apreciado indicios de indebido uso de fondos públicos, y no las medidas para evitar desahucios como el de Maricarmen. Y ha celebrado que la Diputación Permanente de la Cámara baja sacara adelante el decreto este jueves, horas antes del inicio formal de la campaña. “Hemos hecho un poquito mejor a nuestro país”.

Armengol también ha incidido en la vivienda, que se ha convertido en una de las ideas fuerza de los socialistas. “El modelo de Feijóo para la vivienda es Marga Prohens ―la actual presidenta balear―, y eso que desde que gobierna la vivienda de alquiler ha subido un 70% y la gente con salarios dignos en Baleares tiene que vivir en caravanas o habitaciones compartidas”. “Pues bien, el jueves aprobamos el real decreto Maricarmen, que nos orgullece a todos en el Congreso. ¿Y quién votó en contra? El PP y Vox”.

Rosario Sánchez Grau, vicesecretaria general de la federación de Baleares y candidata en mayo a la presidencia del Consell autonómico, ha insistido en la movilización. “La derecha quiere que nos quedemos en casa, pero el 29 de noviembre vamos a votar por fuerza y vamos a ganar las elecciones, porque tenemos el ánimo, la esperanza, la convicción y al mejor candidato, que nos ha inyectado ilusión, fuerza y energía positiva”, ha apuntado y sus palabras han puesto al público en pie. “Gracias por plantarle cara a la derecha, que te lo ha querido hacer pagar muy caro y te ha atacado con la agresividad más cruel y con su odio más miserable, a ti y a tu familia”, le ha dicho a Sánchez.

Iago Negueruela, candidato a la alcaldía de Palma de Mallorca y secretario general de la agrupación municipal socialista, ha reivindicado la regularización de inmigrantes irregulares, cuya crítica es una de las grandes banderas tanto del PP como de Vox. “Hoy, entre nosotros, hay muchas personas que os habéis acogido a la regularización. Eran vecinos y vecinas que vivíais con nosotros. Y hoy además tenéis derechos. Ejerced los derechos que ahora tenéis. Que nadie os invisibilice, que nadie os expulse de una sociedad que os necesita, en la que vivís, en la que trabajáis”, ha proclamado entre vítores. Los mismos que han atronado cuando Sánchez ha posado con un cartel que rezaba La Peter lo peta.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 11/14/2026 - 16:32 Rights groups condemn secret execution of former child protester as a tool of political oppression under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman This picture shows a poster depicting King Salman bin Abdulaziz (R), and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (L) in Riyadh on May 12, 2025 (AFP) Off Saudi Arabia executed a man who was detained as a child, alongside another Saudi national from the Kingdom’s Shia-majority Eastern Province. In a statement on Saturday, the Saudi Press Agency confirmed that Riyadh had executed Jawad Qureiris. Hailing from a prominent Shia-majority family in the Kingdom’s Eastern Province, Qureiris was a former child defendant who was just 14 to 15 years old during the 2011-12 Arab Spring protests. Qureiris’ family has a documented history of encounters with state security: one of his brothers was killed by security forces, while another was arrested at age 13 and faced capital charges related to alleged offences committed when he was nine years old. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Interior also announced that Fadel bin Hassan bin Abdullah Al-Safwani was executed on Saturday. The ministry claimed the men were convicted of “terrorist crimes,” alleging they joined a foreign terrorist organisation, opened fire on security personnel and vehicles with weapons and explosives, possessed live ammunition, and provided logistical and financial support for operations within the Kingdom. According to the SPA statement, the cases passed through specialised criminal courts, where the men’s legal responsibility was established before the verdicts were upheld by the Supreme Court and ratified via a royal decree. Qureiris was arrested in December 2020 and charged with offences related to taking part in protests and organising on social media. The late activist would have been 14 at the time of some of the protests in which he is alleged to have participated. His family said he was severely tortured until he gave a false confession to non-lethal terrorism offences that was used to convict him. Trump says Saudi Arabia is 'disintegrating'  were children at the time of their alleged crimes, all from Shia families in eastern provinces and all executed for offences related to demonstrations during and after the Arab Spring protests in 2011-12. Jeed Basyouni, Reprieve's head of MENA death penalty projects, condemned the executions and said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s “penalty for dissent is death- and we’ve seen very clearly in the last two years that this applies to children too.” “Just like the other four young men executed recently for taking part in demonstrations when they were children, Jawad was tortured into making a false confession to so-called 'terrorist' offences and then tried, convicted, sentenced and finally killed in secret,” said Jeed Basyouni, Reprieve's Head of MENA Death Penalty Projects. “The Crown Prince has pursued a vendetta against Jawad's family and others like it who dared to question his right to rule. This is a regime that uses capital punishment as a tool of political oppression and to settle personal scores. Saudi Arabia’s international partners must not stand by and let this happen, and should make urgent representations to halt the imminent execution of Youssef al Manasif." The Eastern Province, a historic hotbed of anti-government demonstrations and home to the kingdom's vast oil reserves, has long been the focal point of state crackdowns against its Shia-majority population. articles.body:
Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.

The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.

Exclusive analysis of official figures for the Guardian reveals the NHS would have to treat 2,850 additional patients on time each month to get back on track, assuming patient volumes remain consistent.

According to calculations by Radiotherapy UK, 24,400 cancer patients a month would need to start treatment on time to hit the 80% target in March. But the NHS is only treating about 21,500 cancer patients a month within the 62-day target, leaving a monthly shortfall of 2,850 and a cumulative shortfall of 9,490 patients, the charity found.

Prof Pat Price, the chair of Radiotherapy UK and a leading oncologist, said: “The government is going to miss its cancer treatment target because the NHS does not have enough staff or equipment to treat the number of patients coming through its doors. This lack of leadership means thousands more people could die because they don’t get their treatment on time.”

The analysis also found significant disparities between treatment of common cancer types. While more than two-thirds of patients with prostate and breast cancers were treated within two months ((70.1% and 68.8% respectively), only 60.9% of those with lung cancer and 60% of those with gynaecological cancers were treated on time. For head and neck cancers, barely half (56.5%) were. Regional inequalities were also stark, the research found. The Midlands had the lowest proportion treated on time, at 66.6%, compared with 77.3% in London.

Mark Lawler, a professor of digital health and chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, believes failures of accountability and focus are to blame. He said: “The whole system is being held together by goodwill glue alone. Lack of leadership is derailing efforts to improve cancer survival. Unless there is accountability for these failures by the NHS, a radical change in mindset and a focus on the basics, we will miss hitting treatment targets for another decade.”

The figures come as analysis of latest cancer diagnosis targets by Cancer Research UK shows that, over the last year, barely half (55.4%) of patients with cancer were diagnosed within 28 days of an urgent referral, against the faster diagnostic standard target of 80%, compared with 79.1% of patients who received the all-clear on time.

Naser Turabi, Cancer Research UK’s director of health policy and evidence, said hospital capacity was not able to keep pace with surging demand for cancer diagnosis – with urgent referrals in England up about 20% over the past four years alone. “While recent investment in diagnostic equipment is welcome, we’re not seeing enough progress to cut waiting times for the 6% of people who go on to receive a cancer diagnosis,” he said.

Dr Hilary Williams, the Royal College of Physicians clinical vice-president and a consultant in medical oncology, said crucial earlier diagnosis was only beneficial if patients could then be treated quickly.

“To close the gap, the NHS needs sufficient capacity across the whole cancer pathway,” Williams said. “That means more diagnostic capacity, including imaging, endoscopy and pathology, alongside the specialist workforce needed to deliver and interpret those tests. It also means enough treatment capacity in surgery, radiotherapy and systemic treatments so that diagnosing people more quickly doesn’t simply move the bottleneck further down the pathway.”

Dr Stephen Harden, the president of the Royal College of Radiologists, said “chronic shortages” of clinical radiologists and clinical oncologists, who diagnose, monitor and treat cancer, were “driving dangerous delays” in diagnosing and treating the disease.

“Perversely, NHS hiring freezes for these doctors have doubled in the last year, making it even harder to keep patients safe,” Harden said. “Technology and new ways of working can relieve pressure to an extent, but fundamentally, rising demand for cancer care has outpaced workforce capacity. The government must now step in to end recruitment freezes and ensure services have the doctors they need to diagnose and treat patients on time.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction, with all three cancer standards better than a year ago, and around 290,000 more people over the last year getting diagnosed on time or having cancer ruled out, compared to the year before the election.

“But we know there is much more to do. Our national cancer plan will help more people to get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner, giving them the best possible chances of recovery and survival.”

articles.title: US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
articles.summary: Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.
articles.preview: Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia. US negotiators have floated the idea that Ukraine should cede parts of eastern Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after the latest rounds of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi and Ireland. This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
articles.body:
Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.

US negotiators have floated the idea that Ukraine should cede parts of eastern Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after the latest rounds of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi and Ireland.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” he said. “That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda.”

Zelenskyy said the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine the US asked about were areas Russia does not control. The Ukrainian president said he refused to cede territory.

“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

Putin has long said that Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy did say that if Ukraine received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, military and reconstruction funds, and a recovery plan from the US and other partners, he would put the question about ceding parts of Donbas to a national referendum.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said.

He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognising occupied territories as Russian. Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country’s constitution.

“If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in NATO right now anyway.”

Despite the diplomatic push to end the conflict, Russia and Ukraine reported numerous overnight attacks. Russian officials reported on Friday that about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets, while Ukraine reported attacks on a hospital and the port of Odesa.

At the summit in Ireland over recent days, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers – non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland – as well as EU officials. They would hold talks with US and Ukrainian officials, but not with Russia.

articles.title: EU calls for immediate humanitarian access to Gaza
articles.summary: The EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies" after the group was blocked access into Gaza.
articles.preview: The EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies” after the group was blocked access into Gaza. The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.
articles.body:
The EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies” after the group was blocked access into Gaza.

The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.

Civilian infrastructure and medical facilities in Gaza “must be protected,” said an EU statement released on Saturday by the office of Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and the Vice-President of the European Commission.

The EU call came as an Israeli drone attack killed two more Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday.

The drone struck them as they walked down a street in Jabaliya on the northern edge of Gaza City, according to Mohamed Abu Selmiya, director of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, where the casualties were taken. The American field hospital said several other people were wounded but did not provide a number.

The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas “militants” in the area.

An Israeli air attack on Thursday at the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon, and left dozens wounded.

“The EU underlines the need to respect international law, including international humanitarian law, at all times,” the 27-nation bloc said on Saturday. “This includes the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as medical personnel and facilities. The recent airstrike on the Nasser Hospital is deeply alarming,” it added.

Heavy rains

Damage from Israeli attacks on Gaza’s infrastructure has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials and the UN said this week. Gaza’s media office reported that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.

Heavy rain has directly affected at least 106,000 people in Gaza in recent days, according to the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged and latrines overflowing into camps.

In response, the EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies, and humanitarian organisations including NGOs, and comply with all its obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law.”

The EU reaffirmed “its commitment to the two-state solution” and called for “the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza” as it called for “sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale” to ease the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
articles.summary: Trump will discuss the "reduction of nuclear weapons" during the unprecedented talks, a spokeswoman says.
articles.preview: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said. The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
articles.body:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.

Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.

Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.

But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.

Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.

The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.

Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

articles.title: Zelenski asegura que EE UU sugiere admitir a Ucrania en la OTAN a cambio de entregar el Donbás a Rusia
articles.summary: El presidente ucranio descarta esa posibilidad que, afirma, debería ser sometida a referéndum en caso de concretarse una oferta
articles.preview: El presidente ucranio descarta esa posibilidad que, afirma, debería ser sometida a referéndum en caso de concretarse una oferta El presidente de Ucrania, Volodimir Zelenski, ha asegurado que los mediadores de Estados Unidos para ese conflicto han planteado la posibilidad de aceptar al país en la OTAN a cambio de que renuncie al Donbás y se lo entregue a Rusia.
articles.body:
El presidente ucranio descarta esa posibilidad que, afirma, debería ser sometida a referéndum en caso de concretarse una oferta

El presidente de Ucrania, Volodimir Zelenski, ha asegurado que los mediadores de Estados Unidos para ese conflicto han planteado la posibilidad de aceptar al país en la OTAN a cambio de que renuncie al Donbás y se lo entregue a Rusia. Esta es la primera vez que se pone sobre la mesa una posible vinculación del deseo de Ucrania de ingresar en la Alianza con concesiones territoriales, según las declaraciones de Zelenski difundidas por su oficina este sábado.

“Los estadounidenses plantearon una pregunta: “¿Y si Ucrania se une a la OTAN? ¿Se retiraría Ucrania de Donbás?”, ha afirmado el presidente sobre esa posibilidad, que surgió tras la última ronda negociadora entre Rusia y Ucrania, bajo mediación estadounidense, que concluyó el miércoles en Abu Dabi, la capital de Emiratos Árabes Unidos.

“Por eso creo que la OTAN vuelve a estar sobre la mesa. Pero también habéis oído las declaraciones de (el presidente ruso Vladimir) Putin, y se trata de una conversación extremadamente difícil”, ha aseverado el presidente ucranio.

Putin lleva tiempo afirmando que la adhesión de Ucrania a la OTAN es una línea roja para Moscú, y ha citado esta cuestión como una de las razones que a sus ojos justifica la invasión a gran escala de Ucrania que comenzó en 2022.

En sus declaraciones, Zelenski reitera su postura de que Kiev no está dispuesta a ceder territorio. Sin embargo, el presidente ha matizado luego que, si esta propuesta se concreta dentro de un paquete integral que incluya garantías de seguridad, el derecho a un ejército ucranio fuerte y bien financiado, y fondos para la reconstrucción, la sometería a un referéndum nacional. “No tengo derecho a decidirlo yo solo. Necesito concreción, que aún falta, y todo esto se está debatiendo”, ha señalado.

Los enviados estadounidenses para el conflicto en Ucrania, Jared Kushner y Steve Witkoff, viajaron el jueves a Dublín, donde se celebraba una cumbre europea, para reunirse con Zelenski tras los contactos mantenidos el día anterior con el presidente ruso, Vladimir Putin.

Hasta ahora Washington había descartado el ingreso de Ucrania en la OTAN, mientras que Moscú exige neutralidad y límites a las fuerzas militares ucranias, además de la renuncia a territorios, como base para cualquier acuerdo.

Zelenski ha indicado además que los estadounidenses han trasladado a Kiev que Rusia quiere “otra estructura de seguridad diferente” para Europa. “Yo creo que puede ser peligroso (...) Creo que los americanos han planteado esto por influencia rusa”, ha argumentado. Y ha recordado que en 2021 Putin planteó a Joe Biden “la redistribución de fuerzas en Europa y en todo el mundo, debilitar o retirar tropas de la OTAN y la retirada de tropas estadounidenses”.

El mandatario ha corroborado luego los comentarios de los líderes europeos que participaron en la cumbre de Dublín el viernes y rechazado la petición de Rusia de alcanzar un acuerdo sobre ese diseño de la arquitectura de seguridad europea sin poner fin antes a la guerra en Ucrania.

“No podemos dar un vuelco a todo y empezar hablando de cambiar el marco de seguridad en el mundo o en todo el continente en general, y solo entonces poner fin a esta guerra. Primero hay que acabar con la guerra”, ha declarado Zelenski.

El presidente rechaza asimismo la sugerencia de Putin de un alto el fuego humanitario local en Kostiantynivka, una ciudad que ambos contendientes se disputan en la región oriental ucrania de Donetsk, en Ucrania. En opinión de Zelenski, los civiles de esa localidad ya han tenido la oportunidad de salir de ella, por lo que acusó a las fuerzas rusas de enmascarar su incapacidad de tomar la urbe militarmente lanzando la idea de un alto el fuego para así poder apoderarse de la ciudad.

“Putin simplemente quiere que abandonemos Kostiantynivka para que ellos puedan entrar y ocupar toda la ciudad de esa manera”, ha dicho.

“He trasladado mi postura a los negociadores americanos: la gente que hay allí son solo ciudadanos de Ucrania con armas y ciudadanos de Rusia, ocupantes, también con armas”, ha explicado Zelenski.

Ucrania ha facilitado una lista de otros siete u ocho asentamientos en primera línea del frente donde hay civiles, incluidos niños, atrapados, con vistas a una posible tregua humanitaria, pero, ha acusado Zelenski, Rusia prefiere utilizarlos como objetivos militares, una acusación que Moscú niega.

El presidente ucranio además ha puesto como ejemplo la tregua de Oleshki que permitió la evacuación de la población, pero también habilitó a Rusia para reforzar sus posiciones militares.

Por último, ha destacado que durante el mes de octubre Rusia tuvo 54.000 muertos y heridos graves en lo que supone el peor mes para el país desde que empezó la escalada bélica, hace ya casi cinco años.

Abu Dabi

La última ronda negociadora entre Rusia y Ucrania, bajo mediación de Estados Unidos, concluyó el miércoles en Abu Dabi sin ningún avance significativo, aunque las partes acordaron un intercambio de prisioneros que afectará a más de 1.000 personas, según afirmó Zelenski, que precisó que las cifras definitivas del intercambio de prisioneros aún se estaban negociando.

Los enviados estadounidenses Witkoff y Kushner se habían comprometido a plantear a Putin un alto el fuego para detener los ataques a infraestructura energética en su reunión en Moscú el jueves, según afirmó el presidente ucranio, pero tampoco sobre esa cuestión se han divulgado progresos.

Zelenski se reunió con Witkoff y Kushner el jueves en Irlanda tras sus conversaciones en Moscú. En Dublin afirmó que los negociadores estadounidenses le habían comunicado que todas las partes habían acordado que Europa tuviera un puesto en la mesa de negociaciones en las próximas conversaciones de paz.

En Abu Dabi, los representantes de Europa —que es ahora el mayor apoyo financiero y militar de Ucrania— mantuvieron conversaciones con funcionarios estadounidenses y ucranios, pero no se sentaron a la mesa con Rusia. En la cumbre de Irlanda, los líderes de la UE acordaron que el equipo europeo para cualquier ronda de negociaciones de paz sobre Ucrania estaría compuesto por cinco grandes potencias militares —el Reino Unido, que no es miembro de la UE, además de Francia, Alemania, Italia y Polonia— así como por altos funcionarios de la UE.

articles.title: How does Iran view shift in US approach after JD Vance ordered away?
articles.summary: Washington believes maritime blockade, overland border disruptions, air restrictions and isolating sanctions are working
articles.preview: Washington believes maritime blockade, overland border disruptions, air restrictions and isolating sanctions are working. Tehran, Iran – Decision-makers in Iran are now considering the implications of Vice President JD Vance’s removal from the Iran file to focus on domestic issues, which analysts say could increase the chances of conflict between the two sides.
articles.body:
Washington believes maritime blockade, overland border disruptions, air restrictions and isolating sanctions are working.

Tehran, Iran – Decision-makers in Iran are now considering the implications of Vice President JD Vance’s removal from the Iran file to focus on domestic issues, which analysts say could increase the chances of conflict between the two sides.

Vance has been the US’s chief negotiator in talks with Iran, but US President Donald Trump told him to direct his focus on alleged Democratic “corruption”, according to a post by Trump on Truth Social on Thursday. He added that a deal with Iran was no longer a priority for the government.

The vice president is believed to be viewed by Tehran as one of the more pragmatic figures in the Trump administration since the US and Israel launched their surprise war on Iran on February 28.

Nasser Hadian, professor of international relations at the University of Tehran, said that by assigning Vance to the case of alleged domestic corruption, Trump was mainly signalling a confrontation with the Democrats after their sweeping victories against the governing Republican Party in the midterm elections.

But the move may also serve Israel, which is reportedly eager for Trump to launch new strikes against Iran, after Vance blamed the Republicans’ humiliating defeat in the midterms on the war.

“Another signal is to Iran, essentially saying reaching a deal now is not a priority, and that the person known to have a relatively softer stance on Iran was redirected to other issues,” Hadian said.

The negotiator

Vance is believed to have been in favour of a negotiated resolution to the war, due to its rising economic costs for US citizens and their opposition to the war suggested in opinion polls.

The vice president was backed by Trump envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff when he negotiated the now-defunct memorandum of understanding with Iran in June, which briefly paused the war and resumed shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio has, meanwhile, called Iranian authorities “insane” for their demands on ending the war. But he also acknowledged the cost of an all-out war and seeks to win via deepening economic pressure and isolation on all Iranians.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced an impeachment vote due to his role in the war, and Central Command chief Brad Cooper are reportedly in favour of renewed military action against Iran.

Vance wrote a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in late October, as regional mediators redoubled their efforts to bridge gaps between the two sides. Rezaei initially described the tone of the missive as positive, but by last week, he was addressing claims of progress and a possible direct meeting with Vance as “fake news about imaginary talks”.

“You lost the war and the election. Vance has conceded, Rubio is heading for the exit, Hegseth is about to be fired, and the CENTCOM commander is now a podcaster!” he wrote on X at the time.

‘With or without Vance’

Mediated contacts are ongoing between the two sides, but no breakthrough is expected. Tehran is demanding seven conditions and clear sequencing of concessions to end the war, but this is appearing to be unacceptable to the US.

Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies, pointed out that Trump has repeatedly highlighted alleged rifts within the Iranian negotiating team. But he said Iranian authorities were also questioning the reliability of another potential agreement with Washington.

“Even if you can imagine Mr Rezaei sitting down with Mr Vance, and reaching a deal? What guarantee is there that Trump will enforce it?” he told Al Jazeera.

The atmosphere of mistrust between the two sides is also complicating prospects of a deal, he added. This means that the ongoing US siege on Iran and harsh sanctions will continue, something that could cost Iran more than a relatively shorter military conflict with Washington, he added.

“The blockade and disruptions are significantly raising the costs for Iranian people. The current state of no war and no negotiated resolution is very dangerous,” Sedghian said.

Iranian reformist newspaper Shargh argued this week that Vance’s role concerning Iran is unresolved rather than definitely terminated, but also said the conflict could further escalate.

Conservative Farhikhtegan daily disputed the portrayal of Vance as genuinely antiwar, arguing that diplomacy, military force and economic pressure ultimately serve a common objective for the US in trying to coerce Iran to accept its conditions.

For now, the two sides are continuing to fight over control in the Strait of Hormuz, with retaliatory attacks on shipping and military installations.

On Friday and Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and regular army separately claimed several new incidents of vessels either hitting naval mines or being struck by projectiles after attempting “unauthorised” routes in the critical waterway.

The latest weekly report by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) on Friday reported eight incidents in and around the strait, mostly in the southern route near Oman.

UKMTO also recorded 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits through the strait during the week, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels.

Hadian believes that Iranian decision-makers will not tolerate the current situation indefinitely.

“The authorities will either go after their warships, their vessels, or their military bases,” he added. “The stronger the blockade becomes, including through maritime pressure and disruptions for overland borders and air travel, war becomes more probable.”

But Trump’s sidelining of Vance on the Iran issue will not radically alter the current situation, Hadian said, since Washington believes its tactic of economic pressure on Tehran can force it to make concessions.

“The US would have done this with or without Vance, and I believe it will continue to do this,” he said.

articles.title: New facilities in Laos and Cambodia: Is China expanding its military presence in Southeast Asia?
articles.summary: China has been growing its economic relationships in Southeast Asia. Now new military facilities in Laos and Cambodia are causing smaller countries to worry China's military networks are also expanding.
articles.preview: Is China expanding its military presence in Southeast Asia? November 14, 2026 China has been growing its economic relationships in Southeast Asia. Now new military facilities in Laos and Cambodia are causing smaller countries to worry China's military networks are also expanding. It's often said that maintaining good relations with your neighbors is essential. So in early November, China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi invited his counterparts from Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Myanmar to Beijing.
articles.body:
Is China expanding its military presence in Southeast Asia?

November 14, 2026

China has been growing its economic relationships in Southeast Asia. Now new military facilities in Laos and Cambodia are causing smaller countries to worry China's military networks are also expanding.

It's often said that maintaining good relations with your neighbors is essential. So in early November, China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi invited his counterparts from Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Myanmar to Beijing.

There the six countries agreed on closer economic and security cooperation.

The visit is just one example of China's growing influence on Southeast Asia. It's not just about trade or infrastructure either, it's also increasingly about military cooperation.

New airbase in Laos

For instance, at the end of September, China and Laos opened a joint military support and training center north of the Laotian capital, Vientiane. Initially Laotian air force pilots are to be trained at the Ban Keun airfield, China has said.

Earlier in 2025 China expanded its footprint at Cambodia's Ream naval base. China uses the facility on the Gulf of Thailand for logistics and training. And while Japanese and Vietnamese ships can visit the port, they're docked at a southern quay and it's unclear if other navies can use the same facilities under the same conditions as China.

"It remains to be seen how this [Ban Keun] will change China's military access to Southeast Asia," says Marco Bünte, a professor of Asian politics at the University Erlangen Nuremberg in Germany.

In recent years, China has significantly expanded its economic influence in the region.

The China-Laos railway and other infrastructure projects connect Laos more closely with its northern neighbor. Laos is also heavily indebted to China.

Bünte points out that Laos and Cambodia have been close military partners of China for some time and the new facility in Laos can be seen as another step towards deepening cooperation.

If that proves correct, "China would gain strategic depth in mainland Southeast Asia," Bünte explained. "It would also give China better military access to the South China Sea."

Johann Fuhrmann, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's Beijing office, points out that one should distinguish between training Laotian pilots and any potential use of the facilities by Chinese armed forces later.

"China gains influence when it co-designs the training and operation of such facilities over several years," Fuhrmann told DW.

Chinese planes in Laos

But nobody should underestimate China's military positioning, Bünte continued. "China is expanding its military operational capabilities here although I wouldn't speak of military hegemony because China hasn't achieved that yet."

With regard to the Laotian airbase, China says that Laotian pilots will be trained there. But beside military transporters and helicopters, Laos actually only has three light combat aircraft by Russia's Yakovlev works.

According to the aviation media outlet FlightGlobal, four more K-8s, Chinese two-seat intermediate jet trainer and light attack aircrafts, are in service there. Satellite images analyzed by the Reuters news agency in early October show eight K-8s at the base — even thought this doesn't necessarily mean they are stationed there permanently.

Fuhrmann doesn't think anybody should jump to conclusions about this.

"The idea of a Chinese air corridor is more of a future scenario than something that has already been proven," he says.

For example, the runway at Ban Keun is only 2,000 meters (6,562 feet) long, which makes it too short for large Chinese bombers. These usually require 3,000 meters.

The crucial question is what rights China will be granted, Fuhrmann continues: "Will China have to obtain the approval of the respective government for every new use? Or are there longer-term commitments that both sides can invoke, even in times of crisis?"

Surrounding countries are reacting differently to what appears to be China's growing influence in Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar because these countries are already considered closer to China.

Other Southeast Asian nations are hedging, trying to expand their relationship with China without severing ties with the US and also maintaining economic links with other Western nations. China's involvement offers them additional options and Beijing wants to explore those possibilities. That's just pragmatic though, Bünte says of the smaller Asian nations.

"Overall, these states… try to keep as many options open as possible," he notes.

China: 'Not against third parties'

Vietnam and the Philippines are watching developments particularly closely. Both have territorial disputes with China in the South China Sea. But Vietnam also has close historical ties to Laos and trained its own military there.

In early November, the Vietnamese government declared that any military cooperation must serve peace and stability and referred to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, commonly known as the ASEAN Treaty. China is not an ASEAN member but has also stated that its activities are not directed against any third parties.

"So far, these are individual steps," Bünte adds. "We would have to wait and see if this leads to a broader military alliance in the years to come."

Fuhrmann says that Western nations should help strengthen the smaller countries in the region and take their interests seriously.

"Ultimately, a counterweight can only be achieved through tangible contributions, not through warnings or lectures from Europe," he says.

This story was originally published in German.

articles.preview: This is the final edition of the ASEAN Summit before Singapore takes over the chairmanship of the regional bloc next year. MANILA: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong will visit the Philippine capital of Manila to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and related meetings from Nov 15 to Nov 17. It is the second of the ASEAN summits this year, and the final edition before Singapore takes over the chairmanship of the regional bloc in 2027.
articles.body:
This is the final edition of the ASEAN Summit before Singapore takes over the chairmanship of the regional bloc next year.

MANILA: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong will visit the Philippine capital of Manila to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and related meetings from Nov 15 to Nov 17.

It is the second of the ASEAN summits this year, and the final edition before Singapore takes over the chairmanship of the regional bloc in 2027.

During the closing ceremony on Nov 17, there will be a symbolic handover of the ASEAN chairmanship from the Philippines to Singapore. The leader of the outgoing chair typically hands over the ceremonial gavel to the leader of the next chair country.

At the Nov 17 event, Mr Wong will, for the first time, lay out Singapore’s plans for its chairmanship, which officially begins on Jan 1 next year.

The Philippines’ chairmanship theme of Navigating Our Future, Together encapsulates ASEAN’s commitment to deepening integration, strengthening economic cooperation and navigating evolving global challenges with unity and cohesion, said Singapore's Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) in a statement on Saturday.

“The ASEAN leaders will reaffirm their commitment to ASEAN’s community building efforts and discuss ways to promote an open and inclusive regional architecture,” said the PMO about the agenda in Manila.

“They will discuss opportunities in the digital and green economies, including strengthening ASEAN’s energy security and resilience to accelerate the region’s green energy transition and to better withstand external shocks.”

The leaders will also discuss how ASEAN can strengthen its collaboration with external partners to advance peace, stability and prosperity in the region, PMO said.

During the summits, Mr Wong will also meet leaders from ASEAN’s key partners, including Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea, the United States and the United Nations.

Mr Wong will be accompanied on this trip by his wife Mrs Wong and Foreign Affairs Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

In his absence, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) Gan Kim Yong will be the acting prime minister.

Mr Gan was also in Manila on Saturday to join his ASEAN counterparts in inking the bloc's Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA).

articles.title: Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics
articles.summary: The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.
articles.preview: November 14, 2026 The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind. When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.
articles.body:
November 14, 2026

The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Pressure on politicians

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Diplomatic disputes

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

'Hostage diplomacy'

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

Punishing process

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."

This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: South Korea should not fear China's rise, foreign minister says
articles.summary: "We should neither have an unfounded fear of China's rise nor underestimate its capabilities and potential," South Korea's Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said, a day after meeting with Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing.
articles.preview: "We should neither have an unfounded fear of China's rise nor underestimate its capabilities and potential," South Korea's Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said, a day after meeting with Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing. SEOUL: South Korea should neither fear China's rise nor underestimate its capabilities, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on Saturday (Nov 14), urging deeper cooperation ahead of a regional summit in China next week.
articles.body:
"We should neither have an unfounded fear of China's rise nor underestimate its capabilities and potential," South Korea's Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said, a day after meeting with Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing.

SEOUL: South Korea should neither fear China's rise nor underestimate its capabilities, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on Saturday (Nov 14), urging deeper cooperation ahead of a regional summit in China next week.

"During this visit to China, I was reminded that we should neither have an unfounded fear of China's rise nor underestimate its capabilities and potential," Cho wrote on X, saying Seoul should build cooperation benefiting both countries by drawing on the autonomy and creativity of its people and companies.

Cho's remarks came after talks and dinner with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Friday, their first meeting in about three months.

The ministers discussed bilateral ties, issues on the Korean Peninsula and ways to deliver tangible benefits to people in both countries.

The meeting came ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in Shenzhen on Nov 18-19, which South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will attend. Lee is also scheduled to join a dinner hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Seoul has said.

The summit is expected to bring together several major world leaders. US President Donald Trump is set to meet Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin next Thursday on the sidelines of APEC, with nuclear arms reductions among the issues on the agenda, the White House said.

Cho said Seoul would seek to use Lee's visit to advance bilateral ties and expand "horizontal and mutually beneficial" cooperation in areas where the two countries have complementary strengths.

Lee's administration has sought to improve relations with China, South Korea's largest trading partner, after ties were strained under former president Yoon Suk Yeol, while maintaining Seoul's security alliance with the United States.

Wang said on Friday that China wanted to expand cooperation with South Korea in traditional industries and emerging sectors including artificial intelligence and biomedicine. He said bilateral ties had returned to the right track after exchanges between the two countries' leaders.
