articles.title: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.summary: Leaked Russian records reveal a war toll that falls hardest on older men, poorer regions and foreign recruits.
articles.preview: Leaked Russian records reveal a war toll that falls hardest on older men, poorer regions and foreign recruits. Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year. Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.
articles.body:
Leaked Russian records reveal a war toll that falls hardest on older men, poorer regions and foreign recruits.

Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.

Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.

The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.

Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.

Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.

Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.

So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:

What was leaked, and is it genuine?

The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.

The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.

However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.

Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”

However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.

What do the records show?

A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.

The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.

The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.

Where have most of those Russian casualties occurred?

About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.

Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.

After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.

Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.

Who has been killed?

Older men from poorer, often minority regions.

The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.

Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.

Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.

Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.

How many foreign fighters have been killed?

More than 4,000, and possibly far more.

The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.

Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.

Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.

The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.

About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.

Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.

Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.

Why are foreigners fighting for Russia?

Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.

An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.

An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.

The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.

It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.

Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.

One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.

His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”

Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.

In Kenya, where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.

Moscow denies coercing anyone to fight in Ukraine.

What do these casualty figures mean for the war in Ukraine?

They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.

The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.

It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.

Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.

He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

articles.title: Sudan: Misery worsens amid plummeting aid for displaced people
articles.summary: Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.
articles.preview: November 14, 2026 Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan.
articles.body:
November 14, 2026

Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan. Without urgent provision of flexible funding, even more families will have to cope without adequate protection from extreme weather conditions, insecurity, violence and exploitation in the coming months.

According to a recently published joint statement, $2.9 billion (€2.62bn) is needed for the United Nation's Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. This funding is intended to provide life-saving aid to 20.4 million people in Sudan. So far, however, only 47% of the required funds have been raised.

A total of 33.7 million people in the war- and famine-stricken country are dependent on humanitarian aid. Some 15.4 million alone require emergency shelter and basic household items. However, due to a lack of funding, aid organizations have been able to assist only 10%.

More than three and a half years after the war began between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is still the site of the world's largest humanitarian and displacement crisis. About 8.6 million people fled within the country to escape the escalating violence and more than 4.6 million fled to neighboring countries. Another 5.2 million have returned to their regions of origin despite the ongoing war. However, their towns and infrastructure have been destroyed. Fighting, drone strikes and logistical problems further complicate the delivery of humanitarian aid.

Between 40,000 and 250,000 people have been killed. Accurate or updated figures are not available as fighting continues, satellite-based internet communication is curbed, and many aid organizations and observers have left the country.

Donors cut back on funding

"It's hard to imagine how people are supposed to survive," Marina Peter, chairwoman of the Sudan and South Sudan Forum in Germany, told DW. In large parts of the country, people have been cut off from humanitarian aid since the war began. Some have survived by eating roots. According to the Sudan expert, the fact that people are still returning to war zones from neighboring countries is also linked to shortages: Food rations have been drastically cut in refugee camps.

Ivo Körner, Sudan specialist at Caritas International, criticizes the international community for the sharp decline in aid. "Globally, we're seeing a dramatic drop in funding for humanitarian aid," Körner told DW. It's not just the United States that has slashed its contributions; Germany and the European Union are also providing significantly less funding than they did four or five years ago, he said.

In Sudan, Caritas International supports refugees and the communities hosting them with cash assistance, drinking water supplies, basic medical care and seeds. However, Sudan's Caritas' projects in 2026 have been financed exclusively through donations. While Körner hopes for additional funding from the German Foreign Office for Sudan projects, he predicts that funding opportunities will be significantly more limited than in previous years.

According to Sudan expert Marina Peters, the consequences of the crisis are becoming increasingly difficult to assess. "In many parts of the country, people have already been completely cut off from humanitarian aid since the start of the war," she told DW. Peter also notes that child mortality in Sudan is above average. However, it is nearly impossible to determine the actual extent of the crisis more precisely because the warring parties continue to obstruct humanitarian access.

Who should take action?

On October 23, the United Kingdom and 31 other international partners, including Germany, issued a joint statement on the looming famine in Sudan. According to the statement, 19.5 million people — about 41% of the population — are suffering from acute food insecurity. The countries are calling on the warring parties to allow unimpeded access for humanitarian aid and to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure. At the same time, they are demanding an increase in international aid funding.

While Marina Peter welcomes the appeal in principle, she sees a contradiction. "The question is: Who is this appeal actually directed at?" Most of the signatories have themselves systematically cut funding for humanitarian aid and development cooperation. The appeal to the international donor community is thus ultimately directed at the states themselves.

Meanwhile, the Sudanese government based in the country's capital Khartoum — led by General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan's SAF — rejects all warnings of a famine.

In a statement dated October 26, it claims that the food situation in the country is reportedly reassuring and that government reserves and ongoing agricultural production are sufficient to meet demand. According to Khartoum, the warnings from Western countries amount to a politicization of the humanitarian situation.

Peter criticized this statement as "truly cynical and almost perfidious. The government's claim that humanitarian organizations have unrestricted access also does not reflect reality, she said. In many places, aid continues to be obstructed.

Drone attacks exacerbate dangers

In addition to hunger and displacement, the threat to civilians posed by the use of drones is also growing. The Peace for Sudan Platform issued an appeal on November 5 calling for an end to attacks on civilians, markets, hospitals, and water and electricity supplies. In the first three weeks of October alone, at least 306 people were killed in attacks. According to the UN Human Rights Office, drones claimed the lives of at least 1,120 civilians in the first half of 2026.

"Drone strikes are a major problem," Caritas' Körner confirmed. They cause widespread anxiety among the population and often strike civilians. Added to this is the danger to humanitarian workers. This makes local partner organizations all the more important, he said. They enjoy the trust of the local population, are deeply rooted in the regions and in some cases are able to reach areas that international aid workers can hardly access.

This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China: White House
articles.summary: US officials say President Donald Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms reductions and the war in Iran with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, in what would be an unprecedented trilateral meeting.
articles.preview: US officials say President Donald Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms reductions and the war in Iran with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, in what would be an unprecedented trilateral meeting. WASHINGTON: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first-ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday (Nov 13).
articles.body:
US officials say President Donald Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms reductions and the war in Iran with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, in what would be an unprecedented trilateral meeting.

WASHINGTON: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first-ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday (Nov 13).

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran - but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, US officials said.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.

The Kremlin said later on Saturday that the trilateral meet will take place on Nov 19.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.

YALTA REDUX?

The meeting calls back to the 1945 Yalta summit in the Soviet Union, where then-US president Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe.

Zelenskyy has raised the alarm that the meeting in Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like "redistribution of spheres of influence" for the 21st century.

The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the "Western hemisphere" - including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January - but splitting the world among great powers like it's 1945 may not guarantee security.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president's return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

Among other topics, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump's meetings with Xi, the officials said.

"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," a second US senior official said.

The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.

Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.

Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.

articles.title: DR Congo: Bukavu comedy festival offers laughter amid the ongoing conflict
articles.summary: For one week, comedians from the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and the DRC offer residents a moment of relaxation and hope.
articles.preview: Democratic Republic Of Congo The ninth edition of the International Zero Polémique Festival takes place from 9 to 15 November in Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. For one week, comedians from the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire and the DRC take to the stage to celebrate comedy and offer residents a moment of escape in a region deeply affected by armed violence. Bursts of laughter temporarily overshadowed the anxieties of everyday life as spectators gather to watch performances at the Bukavu Comedy Club.
articles.body:
Democratic Republic Of Congo

The ninth edition of the International Zero Polémique Festival takes place from 9 to 15 November in Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

For one week, comedians from the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire and the DRC take to the stage to celebrate comedy and offer residents a moment of escape in a region deeply affected by armed violence.

Bursts of laughter temporarily overshadowed the anxieties of everyday life as spectators gather to watch performances at the Bukavu Comedy Club.

On stage, comedians take turns sharing anecdotes, improvisations, and jokes. Laughter echoes across the room as applause fills the venue.

The festive atmosphere contrasts sharply with the difficulties faced by the population in recent months. For local performers, the enthusiastic response from the audience is a genuine source of satisfaction.

Beyond the artistic performance itself, making people laugh in an environment marked by stress and uncertainty takes on particular significance.

“It is a pleasure to see so many people laughing at your jokes when we are going through stressful and difficult times. Being able to make people laugh really makes me happy,” says Jospin De Mars, a comedian based in Bukavu.

The festival also provides an opportunity to strengthen exchanges between artists of different nationalities as they share their experiences and artistic styles.

For Jojo La Légende, a comedian from the Republic of Congo, the audience's warm response to his performances are among the most memorable aspects of the festival.

“It brings me joy. I am moved to see that these are people who need happiness, people who need laughter. They are happy, they are delighted,” he says.

“Where there are smiles, there is joy, peace, good health and a positive atmosphere,” he adds.

People in the eastern DRC have lived for several decades amid armed conflicts, forced displacement, and successive humanitarian crises.

In Bukavu, which remains under the control of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), uncertainty persists as clashes continue in several surrounding areas.

In this context, cultural and artistic activities take on a significance that goes beyond simple entertainment.

They provide spaces for people to meet, offer a temporary break from isolation and help maintain a sense of social life despite ongoing tensions.

For some spectators, attending these performances is also a way to regain a sense of lightness and a way to recharge.

Joseph Haadi, a resident of Bukavu, explains that these moments allow him to learn, meet new people, and better manage stress.

“Honestly, it sometimes helps me grow and gain knowledge. It also makes us happy when we are stressed, then we come here,” he says.

While humour cannot erase the trauma of war or resolve the difficulties facing residents, it offers a form of collective relief.

For the duration of a performance, everyday worries fade into the background, making room for sharing, smiles, and togetherness.

Beyond the shows, the festival also aims to promote cultural exchanges and encourage encounters between artists from different backgrounds.

By bringing together comedians from several African countries, the event turns laughter into a common language capable of transcending borders and differences.

This international dimension helps position Bukavu within a broader regional cultural landscape, despite its particularly challenging security environment.

Over seven days of performances and encounters, it serves as a reminder that culture retains its importance, even during the most difficult times.

While laughter does not make the war disappear, in a city where the future remains unclear, these shared smiles carry a particular meaning.

They reflect a population that, despite its hardships, continues to find reasons to come together and hold on to hope.

Other images reveal damaged windows, smoke rising from the building and rescue workers moving through hospital corridors. The fire had been extinguished. The attacks affected two major Ukrainian cities, with emergency services responding to fires, damaged buildings and casualties. In Kyiv, the evacuation of patients highlighted the disruption caused when medical facilities are struck, particularly for people with reduced mobility. The incidents come as Russia continues its aerial attacks on Ukraine more than four years after launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.summary: The 47th Cairo International Film Festival got underway on Wednesday in the Egyptian capital. The event brings together filmmakers, actors and other prominent figures from around the world. This year’s festival is taking place under the shadow of the Middle East war.

The event brings together filmmakers, actors and other prominent figures from around the world. This year’s festival is taking place under the shadow of the Middle East war. articles.body:
Egypt

The 47th Cairo International Film Festival got underway on Wednesday in the Egyptian capital. The event brings together filmmakers, actors and other prominent figures from around the world.

This year’s festival is taking place under the shadow of the Middle East war.

Screenwriter, poet, and producer Medhat El-Adl was honoured with a Golden Pyramid for lifetime achievement.

He says the war affects whether audiences are able to see the films being produced:

"Of course, any war, conflict zone, or tension doesn't just affect cinema, it impacts people's livelihoods. Consequently, people will prioritise earning a living over going to the movie theater. So it has had a very strong impact on everything. If I have 10 cents, will I buy food or spend it on a movie ticket? I'll buy food! So it has affected us in one way or another, and that's just financially speaking.”

The financial situation is pushing production costs through the roof, with no guarantee the outlay will be recovered, says Egyptian actress Gehad Hossam:

"The war is affecting the entire region, the economics of the industry have been impacted because something you used to produce, per say, for 5 EGP suddenly costs 10 EGP, while the market can't absorb or cover that cost increase. It's a tough situation.”

For film critic Tarek El-Shinnawi, Egypt’s film industry faces other challenges - notably restrictions on free speech that limit what filmmakers are able to express:

"We just need the ceiling of censorship to be a bit higher, what Egypt lacks is a censor with a broader horizon, and to open the door for discussing all issues, a great film isn't the one with a high budget or a massive production cost - no, a great film is one that carries an idea and offers freedom to the creator.”

For festival president Hussein Fahmi, the event isn’t only about showcasing contemporary films but also preserving Egypt’s cultural heritage:

"Cinema is not simply entertainment but a record of human experience, social transformations, and historical moments, preserving stories and emotions for generations to come," Fahmi said in his opening remarks.

The festival runs until 20 November.

articles.body:
L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.

Questi episodi si inseriscono in un quadro che ha riportato l’attenzione sulle minacce informatiche e la capacità dell’Italia di contrastarle efficacemente. Il 7 novembre il ministero degli Esteri aveva reso nota la diffusione sul dark web di dati personali del ministro Antonio Tajani. Il Ministro ha collegato le minacce alla posizione italiana sulla guerra in Ucraina e ha chiesto di affrontare il tema delle minacce ibride al G7 degli Esteri, che si è svolto a Parigi il 9 e 10 novembre. Un altro episodio era stato registrato a inizio novembre, quando alcuni supermercati italiani erano stati colpiti da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione, sui cui il governo aveva fatto il punto in una riunione il 3 novembre.

Il 9 novembre il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto, in un’intervista al Corriere della Sera, ha definito la guerra ibrida una «sfida epocale», che deve essere affrontata tramite una strategia comune tra le istituzioni. Una posizione in linea con quanto detto qualche giorno dalla presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni, che aveva richiamato l’attenzione sui possibili effetti degli attacchi informatici, sottolineando i rischi per le infrastrutture civili.

Negli ultimi anni, l’Italia ha introdotto nuove regole, istituito strutture dedicate alla cybersicurezza e stanziato risorse per proteggere le proprie infrastrutture digitali. Ma quali interventi sono stati realizzati e che cosa dicono i dati disponibili sulla loro efficacia?

articles.title: Che cosa ha deciso la Corte costituzionale su Giusi Bartolozzi
articles.summary: È stato accolto solo in parte il conflitto di attribuzione sollevato dalla Camera, e ora l’ex capa di gabinetto di Nordio potrà essere processata per false dichiarazioni
articles.preview: Che cosa succede adesso La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali.
articles.body:
Che cosa succede adesso

La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. In quel caso, la Corte costituzionale dovrebbe verificare se la valutazione dei magistrati abbia leso le prerogative della Camera, non accertare la responsabilità penale di Bartolozzi.

Quanto alle presunte false informazioni, il procedimento prosegue secondo le regole ordinarie, senza necessità di autorizzazione parlamentare. La Procura ha già emesso un decreto di citazione diretta a giudizio nei confronti di Bartolozzi, che quindi potrà andare a processo.

Resta da chiarire se Bartolozzi avrebbe dovuto essere ascoltata come indagata, anziché come persona informata sui fatti. In quest’ultimo caso era tenuta a dire la verità, ed è proprio dalle dichiarazioni rese in questa veste che è nata l’accusa di false informazioni. Se fosse stata ascoltata come indagata, avrebbe invece avuto il diritto di non rispondere. La Corte costituzionale ha lasciato aperta la questione delle eventuali conseguenze sui suoi diritti di difesa. La procura prospetta, dal canto suo, un’altra eventualità: se nel corso del giudizio per false informazioni dovessero emergere indizi di concorso nei reati attribuiti a Nordio, il giudice dovrebbe assolvere Bartolozzi e restituire gli atti al pubblico ministero, per avviare la procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. Anche su questo profilo la Corte non si è pronunciata.

articles.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

articles.body:
November 14, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

Questi i messaggi comparsi nelle ultime ore e in modo massivo sulle pagine social di alcuni politici italiani, dal leader della Lega Matteo Salvini agli eurodeputati di FdI e Pd, Carlo Fidanza e Dario Nardella. La "rivolta dei bot contro i politici", la chiama Repubblica.it che mette in relazione i commenti seriali proveniente da "account sospetti" con il recente malfunzionamento di Microsoft e dei software di intelligenza artificiale (OpenAI e Anthropic). La reazione della politica non si fa attendere, con il vicepremier Matteo Salvini che punta il dito: "Profili falsi arrivavano sui profili della Lega ad insultare e sulle pagine del Pd a glorificare. Vediamo chi c'è dietro. Voglio che siano le forze dell'ordine a capire. Spero che nessuno in questo caso tiri fuori gli hacker russi...". Ancor più duro il senatore Claudio Borghi secondo cui "è bastato un malfunzionamento per scoprire che, invece degli hacker russi, ci sono italianissimi personaggi ad inquinare il dibattito politico con schiere di bot addestrati per attaccare, guarda caso, la Lega e Matteo Salvini. In realtà la cosa non ci stupisce particolarmente: da tempo erano emerse notizie di squadre informatiche addestrate da PD, M5S e persino dalla UE per coordinare gli attacchi contro gli avversari politici". Ma anche Avs chiede chiarezza. Angelo Bonelli riferisce di essere stato lui per primo vittima di questo fenomeno: "I miei profili sono costantemente assaliti da commenti minacciosi e insultanti". Di qui l'auspicio di un inchiesta della magistratura sulle "reti di account automatizzati che usano l'intelligenza artificiale per condizionare il dibattito politico". In questo caso "i bot, per errore, hanno pubblicato la risposta con cui l'IA si rifiutava di scrivere messaggi di propaganda o di insulti contro un partito.

Visualizza questo post su Instagram

Chi sono i mandanti? - si domanda l'esponente dei Verdi - Chi utilizza questi bot in maniera così massiccia e con quali soldi? E perché proprio alla vigilia delle elezioni? Sono domande che riguardano la tenuta della nostra democrazia". Si unisce all'appello Elisabetta Piccolotti: "Non accettiamo che anche la prossima campagna elettorale si svolga in un mare di immondizia", servono "norme tese ad assicurare una par condicio digitale per le prossime elezioni: le piattaforme vanno obbligate a cancellare o sterilizzare i bot, i contenuti prodotti con l'intelligenza artificiale vanno resi chiaramente identificabili, le operazioni dall'estero vanno fermate e il regolamento europeo sulla pubblicità politica deve essere attuato individuando l'agenzia deputata ai controlli e alle sanzioni".

articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.

articles.body:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.

Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

OpenAI has taken several stumbles

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “super app.” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

Apple’s Siri AI

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs. This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Character.ai

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.

But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Relay

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.

The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

Ollie

Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.

However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.

Microsoft’s Recall

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22.

Humane AI Pin

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

Rabbit R1

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down.

articles.summary: Some governments moved to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
articles.preview: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.

China

China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.

Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters’ review of procurement notices, investment plans and corporate disclosures. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.

Singapore

In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.

In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.

South Korea

South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.

Taiwan

Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.

Japan

In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.
